issues.issue: The Monitoring Committee is given authority over "all aspects of this and all similar Consent Judgments", but "similar" and "all aspects" set no boundary on the delegated power. A dispute over the Committee's authority would turn on those words.

The release is triggered by "payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant", but paragraph 3 defines that amount as Defendant's payment aggregated with funds from other institutions, so the condition may be one Defendant alone cannot satisfy.

As with paragraph 9, the state releases become effective on "payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant", a term paragraph 3 appears to define as the pooled multi-institution fund rather than Defendant's own contribution.

The paragraph says Exhibit H obligations "are in addition to" all other obligations and then immediately carves out an offset for wrongful-foreclosure payments; the general additive rule and the specific offset pull against each other, and the scope of "a payment ... for a wrongful foreclosure" is undefined.

The offset operates against "any payment from the Borrower Payment Amount" under paragraph 4, whose distribution is governed by Exhibit C and the State members of the Monitoring Committee, leaving unclear how a federal SCRA payment is to be reduced by a state-administered payment.

The withdrawal right turns on failure to make "Consumer Relief Payments (as that term is defined in Exhibit F)", a defined term that does not appear in paragraph 5's description of the consumer relief obligation, so the triggering default is uncertain.

A party's unilateral power to "declare it null and void with respect to that party" cannot easily be squared with paragraph 13, under which this Consent Judgment "may be modified only by order of this Court".

Retention of jurisdiction "for the duration of this Consent Judgment" sits against paragraph 15, which extends the Court's jurisdiction six months past the Term for violations identified in the final Monitor Report, and against paragraph 12's unilateral withdrawal right.

The Effective Date depends on the judgment being "final and non-appealable", deemed satisfied "if there is no party with a right to appeal the order on the day it is entered" — a self-referential test that does not address intervenors or non-parties.

The paragraph says Defendant "shall have no further obligations" six months after the Term while simultaneously preserving the Court's power to enforce or remedy outstanding violations, and it does not say how a violation must be "identified in the final Monitor Report" to survive. Both the sunset and its exception are open to competing readings.

The extended post-Term jurisdiction here is broader than paragraph 13's retention of jurisdiction "for the duration of this Consent Judgment", and the reference to violations not "cured during the Term" imports Exhibit E's cure machinery referenced in paragraph 2.

A savings clause preserving Defendant's duty to "comply with applicable state and federal law" can be read to cut against the breadth of the releases in paragraphs 9 and 10 (Exhibits F and G), which release specified statutory claims.

The clause calls the operative judgment a "summary document" whose "sum and substance" is reflected herein and in the Exhibits, without saying whether extrinsic material is excluded; "conflict" between Exhibits and paragraphs 1-18 is likewise undefined.

Because the Exhibits are made to govern over paragraphs 1-18, this clause determines whether paragraph 2's flat compliance duty or Exhibit E's enforcement and metrics regime controls, and so is the hinge of any conflict argument in the instrument.
